title: AI knowledge SSOT — training systems/infra + history/lineage
name: systems-history
summary: Reference dictionary slice of the AI knowledge SSOT: (A) the systems/infra layer that makes large-model training and serving tractable, and (B) the dated lineage from the 1958 perceptron through the reasoning-model and MoE-at-scale eras.
note: Compiled from model knowledge; dates cross-checked, no fabrication. Each leaf is one dense English-term sentence (<=220 chars). For ingestion as a child node under the hexa-codex architecture tree, NOT a replacement for any existing node.

children.name: training-systems
children.title: Training systems & infrastructure
children.summary: Parallelism, memory, kernel, serving, queueing, and hardware substrate behind large-model training and inference.

children.name: data-parallelism
children.summary: Data parallelism replicates the whole model per device, splits the global batch across them, and averages gradients by all-reduce each step; near-linear throughput but capped by per-device memory holding the full model.

children.name: model-parallelism
children.summary: Model (inter-op) parallelism partitions a model's layers across devices so one model spans many GPUs, lifting the single-device memory cap at the cost of cross-device activation transfer and pipeline-bubble idle time.

children.name: tensor-parallelism
children.summary: Tensor (intra-op) parallelism shards weight matrices row/column-wise across devices, computing matmuls in parallel and stitching via all-reduce/all-gather; communication-heavy, so kept within a fast NVLink island.

children.name: pipeline-parallelism
children.summary: Pipeline parallelism maps contiguous layer stages to devices and streams micro-batches through them (GPipe/1F1B), trading a startup/drain bubble to train models larger than one device while keeping stages busy.

children.name: sequence-parallelism
children.summary: Sequence/context parallelism splits the token dimension across devices (sharded LayerNorm/dropout, Ring/Ulysses attention), cutting activation memory for very long contexts that tensor parallelism alone cannot fit.

children.name: zero-fsdp-deepspeed
children.summary: ZeRO (DeepSpeed) and PyTorch FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel ranks (ZeRO 1/2/3), gathering each shard per layer for model-parallel savings with a data-parallel API.

children.name: megatron-lm
children.summary: Megatron-LM is NVIDIA's reference framework composing tensor + pipeline + data parallelism (3D, often with ZeRO) plus fused kernels to train transformer LLMs efficiently across thousands of GPUs.

children.name: gradient-accumulation
children.summary: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several forward/backward micro-batches before one optimizer step, emulating a large effective batch on limited memory at the cost of more steps per weight update.

children.name: activation-checkpointing
children.summary: Activation (gradient) checkpointing discards intermediate activations in the forward pass and recomputes them in backward, trading roughly one extra forward of compute for a large cut in peak activation memory.

children.name: mixed-precision-training
children.summary: Mixed-precision training runs matmuls in 16-bit (FP16/BF16, now FP8) while keeping FP32 master weights and (for FP16) loss scaling, roughly halving memory/bandwidth and using tensor cores with little accuracy loss.

children.name: collective-all-reduce
children.summary: Distributed training relies on collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast) via NCCL with ring/tree algorithms over NVLink/InfiniBand; gradient all-reduce dominates synchronous data-parallel traffic.

children.name: accelerators-hbm-memory-wall
children.summary: GPUs/TPUs and other accelerators pair many parallel ALUs with high-bandwidth memory (HBM); since FLOPs grow faster than bandwidth, large-model speed is increasingly bound by the memory wall, not raw arithmetic.

children.name: kernel-fusion-flashattention
children.summary: Kernel fusion merges ops into one GPU kernel to cut HBM round-trips; FlashAttention is the canonical case, an IO-aware tiled kernel that never materializes the full score matrix, making attention memory-linear.

children.name: vllm-pagedattention
children.summary: vLLM serves LLMs with PagedAttention, storing the KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (OS-style paging) to nearly eliminate fragmentation, enabling high-throughput continuous batching and KV sharing.

children.name: batching-throughput-vs-latency
children.summary: Inference trades throughput against latency: bigger/continuous batches amortize weight loads but add queueing delay, so capacity is sized via queueing theory (M/M/c, Erlang-C) for a tail-latency SLO (hexa-codex OPS).

children.name: roofline-model
children.summary: The roofline model plots attainable FLOP/s vs arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte): low-intensity kernels are bandwidth-bound and high-intensity ones compute-bound, diagnosing whether to fuse/recompute or add FLOPs.

children.name: training-cost-economics
children.summary: Training cost is GPU-hours × price, driven by total FLOPs (~6·N·D for N params over D tokens), achieved utilization (MFU), interconnect efficiency, and restart overhead; frontier runs reach tens of millions of dollars.

children.name: domestic-silicon-ascend
children.summary: Sovereign/domestic accelerators (Huawei Ascend with CANN, Google TPU, AWS Trainium/Inferentia) pursue non-NVIDIA capacity, trading a less mature software stack for supply-chain and export-control independence.

children.name: history-lineage
children.title: AI history & lineage
children.summary: Dated lineage of the ideas and models leading to modern LLMs, from the 1958 perceptron to the reasoning-model and MoE-at-scale eras.

children.name: perceptron-1958
children.summary: In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt introduced the perceptron, a trainable single-layer linear threshold classifier; its inability to learn XOR (Minsky & Papert, 1969) helped trigger the first AI winter.

children.name: backprop-1986
children.summary: Backpropagation, efficient chain-rule gradient computation through layers, was popularized for neural nets by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams in 1986, making multi-layer deep networks trainable.

children.name: cnn-lenet-alexnet-1989-2012
children.summary: Convolutional nets matured from LeCun's backprop-trained digit recognizer (LeNet, ~1989/1998) to AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 2012), whose GPU ImageNet win launched the deep-learning boom.

children.name: word2vec-embeddings-2013
children.summary: In 2013 Mikolov et al. released word2vec (skip-gram/CBOW), learning dense distributed word embeddings whose vector geometry captures semantic and analogical relations, establishing learned representations in NLP.

children.name: seq2seq-attention-2014
children.summary: In 2014 Sutskever et al. introduced sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder RNNs, and Bahdanau et al. added attention letting the decoder soft-align to encoder states, fixing the fixed-vector bottleneck in translation.

children.name: transformer-2017
children.summary: The 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al.) introduced the Transformer, replacing recurrence with stacked self-attention and feed-forward blocks; its parallelizable architecture became the LLM backbone.

children.name: bert-gpt-2018
children.summary: In 2018 two transformer pretraining paradigms emerged: OpenAI's GPT (autoregressive decoder, generative) and Google's BERT (bidirectional masked-LM encoder), establishing self-supervised pretrain-then-finetune.

children.name: scaling-laws-gpt3-2020
children.summary: In 2020 Kaplan et al. published neural scaling laws (loss as a power law in params, data, compute) and OpenAI's 175B-parameter GPT-3 showed strong few-shot in-context learning, validating scale as a primary lever.

children.name: instructgpt-rlhf-2022
children.summary: In 2022 OpenAI's InstructGPT showed reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) — instruction tuning plus a learned reward model optimized with PPO — aligns outputs to human intent far better than scale alone.

children.name: chatgpt-moment-2022
children.summary: ChatGPT, released November 2022, packaged an RLHF-tuned GPT-3.5 as a free conversational interface and reached ~100M users within two months, igniting mainstream awareness and the generative-AI race.

children.name: open-weight-era-2023
children.summary: From Meta's LLaMA (Feb 2023) and openly licensed Llama 2 (July 2023), alongside Mistral, Falcon, and later Qwen/DeepSeek, downloadable open-weight models enabled local finetuning and a fast community ecosystem.

children.name: reasoning-model-era-2024
children.summary: From late 2024 the reasoning-model era began with OpenAI's o1 (then o3, DeepSeek-R1), spending extra inference-time compute on long RL-trained chain-of-thought, sharply improving math, coding, and multi-step reasoning.

children.name: moe-at-scale-era
children.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling, popularized by GShard/Switch Transformer and reaching the frontier with Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3, routes each token to a few of many expert FFNs: huge params, low active cost.
